Stereo Pose Pipeline — Weekly Report

Date: 2026-06-29  |  Focus: 3D Human Pose Estimation + Ergonomic Assessment

This week: Research Overview Fanbo7 (Close range) Fanbo4 (Far range) Fanbo3 (Full-body walking) Summary

Research Overview

This week we used three datasets of increasing difficulty as progressive stress tests to validate improvements to the SKT pipeline:

  1. Fanbo7 (~180 cm, single right elbow): Diagnose failures in the existing filter+smooth chain and upgrade the 2D pose model;
  2. Fanbo4 (~410 cm, single right elbow): Expose the physical noise floor of stereo triangulation at long range, and validate bone-length constraints + smoothing as a compensation strategy;
  3. Fanbo3 (walking, 8 joints, full body): Extend the above methods to full-body motion and perform a generalisation sanity check with error attribution.

1. Fanbo7: Pipeline Reconstruction + Model Upgrade

1.1 Starting point: the legacy pipeline's failure mode

The v1 baseline produced 15 angle jumps (>10°) for the right elbow in Fanbo7, with an overall MAE of 6.84° against FastSAM3D. The angle-vs-time trace below shows the characteristic instability:

Frame-by-frame diagnosis showed that 0% of the jumps were caused by calibration, person-matching, or epipolar issues — all failures traced back to 3D depth noise and the pipeline chain itself. A key experiment: disabling the quality filter entirely made the overall bias larger but eliminated the jumps. This proved the jumps were artificially generated by the legacy chain.

1.2 What changed — and why the old chain was wrong

Legacy chain (discarded):

quality filter → set bad frames to NaN → linear interpolation (fill_short_gaps) → moving average → restore NaN

This chain has a fundamental bug: the v1 quality filter uses only a binary pass/fail threshold — frames with moderate (but not terrible) confidence are discarded outright and set to NaN. Then fill_short_gaps draws a straight line across the NaN gap; when moving_average blends across that artificial straight line and the real signal on either side, it creates large jumps at the filter boundary that did not exist in the raw data. The drop-fill-smooth three-step sequence is itself the source of the problem.

New chain:

quality-aware repair → keypoint-level Savitzky-Golay smoothing
  • Quality-aware repair: frames are classified into three tiers — valid (high quality, kept as-is), repairable (moderate quality, temporarily set to NaN then reconstructed by interpolation from neighbouring valid frames), and invalid (severely degraded, set to NaN and not repaired). Compared to v1's binary filter, repairable frames are no longer wasted, the number of usable frames increases, and the large NaN gaps that produced artificial straight lines are eliminated;
  • Keypoint-level Savgol smoothing: smoothing is applied directly to the 3D XYZ coordinates, not to derived joint angles. Because angles are a non-linear function of coordinates, smoothing in coordinate space and then computing angles is geometrically more consistent than smoothing angles directly, and avoids the phase distortion that angle-domain smoothing can introduce. Savgol's local polynomial fit also preserves true motion peaks that a moving average would clip.

The 2D detector was simultaneously upgraded from YOLOv8m-pose to YOLO11l-pose, improving keypoint consistency between left and right views and reducing triangulation mismatches at the source.

Takeaway 1: The YOLO11l upgrade improves left/right view consistency, reducing triangulation noise at the source. The pipeline reconstruction (quality-aware repair + keypoint-level Savgol) eliminates the artificial jumps created by the legacy filter-fill-average chain — this is the primary reason MAE dropped from 6.84° to 2.43°.

2. Fanbo4: The Physical Noise Limit at Long Range

2.1 The challenge of distance

Fanbo4 uses the same "right elbow flex/extend" task, but the subject stands at ~410 cm instead of Fanbo7's ~180 cm. The contrast is immediately visible in the camera frames:

Beyond the visual scale reduction, the more fundamental issue is that stereo depth uncertainty grows quadratically with distance:

σ_z = Z² / (f · B) · σ_disparity

With f = 1500 px, B = 41 cm, σ_disparity ≈ 0.5 px:

  • Fanbo7 (Z = 180 cm): σ_z ≈ 0.4 cm
  • Fanbo4 (Z = 410 cm): σ_z ≈ 1.4 cm (≈ 3.5× more depth noise)

This means that even with identical 2D detection quality, Fanbo4's 3D keypoints inherently jitter 3.5× more in the depth direction. The Stage 1 baseline MAE for Fanbo4 was 15.49°.

2.2 Bone-length soft constraint

The underlying insight is that a person's upper-arm and forearm lengths are physically fixed — they do not change frame to frame. We exploit this as a prior to stabilise the noisy 3D estimates.

In practice: the per-bone length priors are automatically estimated from the most stable frames at the start of the session (IQR-trimmed median — no manual input required). Then, for each frame, instead of solving the unconstrained triangulation, we jointly minimise the reprojection error and penalise deviations from the bone-length prior. The penalty weight λ controls the trade-off; λ = 3.0 was optimal for Fanbo4.

Intuitively, this converts a "3 degrees of freedom in 3D space" problem into a softer "constrained to a bone-length sphere" problem, which is particularly effective at suppressing the high-variance depth (Z) component.

2.3 Savitzky-Golay smoothing

After the bone constraint stabilises per-frame bone lengths, residual high-frequency jitter across frames is handled by Savitzky-Golay (Savgol) smoothing applied at the keypoint coordinate level:

  • Fits a local polynomial within a sliding window (7 frames ≈ 0.56 s) rather than a box average, which preserves the shape of the motion curve (peaks are not clipped);
  • Applied to raw 3D coordinates — not to derived angles — so angle continuity follows naturally.

2.4 Fanbo4 results

ConfigurationMAE vs FastSAM3DJumps (>10°)
Original SKT15.49°5
Bone only (λ = 1.0)11.21°35
Bone (λ=1.0) + Savgol (window 7)11.24°3
Bone (λ=3.0) + Savgol (window 7)9.80°2
Why ~10° residual remains: Even with bone constraints and smoothing, MAE stays near 10°. This residual has two root causes: (1) the physical depth noise floor at Z=410 cm (σ_z ≈ 1.4 cm per frame ≈ 3° angle error for a 25 cm upper arm); (2) a systematic YOLO detection bias on nearly-extended arms at long range — the detector tends to slightly misplace the wrist, artificially increasing the measured flexion by ~5–7°. Neither of these can be resolved by post-processing alone.
Takeaway 2: Bone constraint + Savgol reduces Fanbo4 MAE from 15.49° to 9.80° (−37%) and cuts jump count from 5 to 2. Bone-length priors are an effective compensation for long-range depth noise. The residual ~10° reflects the hard physical and 2D-model limit at this distance.

3. Fanbo3: Full-Body Walking — Generalisation Test

3.1 Why this dataset

Fanbo3 is a ~53 s walking round-trip (≈22 s valid segment) covering 8 joints across the whole body (shoulder, elbow, hip, knee — left and right). It tests whether the bone+Savgol approach generalised from the single-joint elbow case to full-body motion. Both a FastSAM3D TRC and an Xsens MVNX are available, enabling a three-way comparison.

3.4 Error attribution

Elbows (SKT MAE 20–32°) — largest error, clear root cause. Xsens reports ~10° flexion during walking (arm mostly extended — physically correct). SKT reports 30–43°, interpreting the arm as persistently bent. The root cause is YOLO wrist mislocalisation during arm swing: the wrist keypoint is placed near the hip rather than at the hand, making the "forearm" appear to point downward instead of forward, which inflates the computed flexion angle. FastSAM3D achieves only 12.8–13.8° MAE vs Xsens — confirming the problem is in SKT's 2D detection, not in the Kabsch alignment or Xsens calibration.

Shoulders (SKT MAE 11–14°) — systematic positive bias. SKT consistently over-estimates shoulder elevation by ~11–14°. The shoulder angle uses the torso midline (hip_mid → shoulder_mid) as reference; in the camera coordinate frame this direction has a systematic offset relative to Xsens's anatomical definition. FastSAM3D shows only 5.9–6.0° MAE — close to the reference uncertainty — demonstrating this is a SKT-specific frame-definition issue rather than a hard signal-quality limit.

Hips and knees (SKT MAE 11–16°) — mixed causes. FastSAM3D achieves 4.6° for hips (much better than SKT's 10–11°), indicating that SKT's hip estimate is genuinely noisy. For knees, FastSAM3D and SKT are nearly equal (~13°), suggesting that this residual reflects the difficulty of dynamic knee tracking during walking (self-occlusion, fast angular velocity) rather than a SKT-specific failure.

Takeaway 3: Bone + Savgol reduces jump count by 62% and improves smoothness substantially, but does not close the gap between SKT and FastSAM3D for absolute angle accuracy — especially at the elbows (SKT 20–32° vs FastSAM3D 12–14° vs Xsens). The dominant error source is 2D keypoint mislocalisation during arm swing, which is a 2D detector limitation that post-processing cannot correct.

Key findings

  1. Pipeline reconstruction is the biggest lever: The legacy filter→fill→moving_average chain was generating artificial jumps. Replacing it with quality-aware repair + Savgol took Fanbo7 from 6.84° to 2.43°.
  2. Bone constraints compensate for long-range depth noise: Fanbo4 improved from 15.49° to 9.80°; session-specific priors are estimated automatically from stable frames — no manual measurement required.
  3. Full-body walking is limited by 2D detection: For Fanbo3, the dominant error is YOLO wrist mislocalisation during arm swing. FastSAM3D's substantially lower error (9.2° vs SKT's 16.3° on average) confirms this is a 2D detector limitation, not a stereo geometry limitation.
